entity: Commission of Outdoor Recreation, Commonwealth of Virginia
stance_basis: letter urging caution about ORV use where impacts are not fully understood, with specific concerns about wildlife harassment and weaknesses in the draft EIS
summary: The Commission of Outdoor Recreation, Commonwealth of Virginia, submitted a formal letter expressing concern that the environmental impacts of ORV use are not fully understood, criticizing the draft EIS for vague and undocumented impact statements, and urging that great care be taken not to allow ORV use where impacts are uncertain. They specifically raised concern about the opening of roads in Acadia National Park to over-snow vehicles and the potential harassment of wildlife during winter months.
complaint_summary: The Commission criticizes the draft EIS for vague and undocumented impact statements, argues it is fatally weak for covering all ORV types including uninvented ones, and urges that ORV use not be permitted where impacts are not fully understood, citing specific concern about wildlife harassment from over-snow vehicles in Acadia National Park.

statement.text:
We have been giving serious consideration to the many public land management problems which must be solved because of the growing popularity of recreational use of off-road vehicles. • believe the impact of these vehicles on the environment is not fully understood at this time. The draft environmental statement enclosed with Mr. Hofe's letter of June 1, 1972, reinforces our feelings, particularly in those sections that outline the damages which may be done.
In commenting on the statement we would suggest that it repeatedly points out possible impacts without stating that one thing or another will happen. For example, to say "there is reason to believe that family relationships are strengthened by these activities," is hardly a documented statement of favorable impact upon the environment. Another we note for your consideration is that, "use of over-snow vehicles for fishing purposes may result in some water pollution from the litter and waste left on the ice." We have every reason to believe pollution will occur.
A fatal weakness of the statement is that it pertains to all types of off-road vehicles, even those at this time not invented. We would suggest an impact statement should be made regarding each type vehicle in its most common use environment.

In closing, we suggest that great care should be taken not to allow use where the impact is not fully understood or where the local land manager believes no harm will be done. An example of the type of permitted use that concerns us is the opening of selected roads in Acadia National Park to over the snow vehicles. While it is probably true that little or no damage will be done to the roads so used, we would be concerned about the harrassment of wildlife of the park. During the winter months land animals are under great stress in finding food and shelter and great rafts of migratory waterfowl numbering in the thousands of birds nest and feed off shore if not disturbed.
Thank you for asking for our comments.
Sincerely,
Rob R. Blackmore
Director
